name: Revision rhinoplasty

card.summary: A second (or later) operation to correct problems from a previous nose job; revision rates are documented and the procedure often needs grafts.
card.note: Technically more complex than primary surgery; body dysmorphic disorder symptoms are common in people seeking rhinoplasty.

quick.overview:
Revision rhinoplasty is surgery to fix aesthetic or functional problems after a previous rhinoplasty, such as tip drop, asymmetry, collapse or breathing difficulty. Wikipedia puts the share of primary operations needing revision at 5 to 20 percent.

On looksmax.org, members ask whether a drooping tip a year after surgery needs a full redo or a minor closed procedure, and discuss other factors such as jaw support.
quick.mechanism: Revisions are usually done by an open approach and often require cartilage from the ear or rib, or implants. Literature covers conchal cartilage grafts for valve collapse, irradiated costal cartilage, Gore-Tex, porous polyethylene and silicone implants.
quick.risks: Reports describe complications from implants and graft materials, persisting obstruction, and dissatisfaction. A study of rhinoplasty candidates found high prevalence of body dysmorphic disorder symptoms.

lead: Revision rhinoplasty, also called secondary rhinoplasty or a redo nose job, is an operation on the nose performed after an earlier rhinoplasty to improve a result that is aesthetically or functionally unsatisfactory. For someone whose first operation left an asymmetric bridge, a pinched or dropped tip, a visible bump above the tip or a nose that is harder to breathe through, a revision is the route by which surgeons aim to restore a balanced profile and a working airway. General references give 5 to 20 percent as the share of primary rhinoplasties that lead to a further operation, and a review of risks and complications puts the figure at roughly 5 to 15 percent [1][2][3].

Revisions are generally regarded by surgeons as more demanding than first-time surgery, because the supporting cartilage and soft tissue have already been altered, scarred or removed. Surgeons therefore commonly work through an open approach and rebuild support with cartilage grafts, taken from the septum, the ear or the rib, and sometimes with donor cartilage or synthetic implants [1][4]. The literature on these materials includes long retrospective series on Gore-Tex, porous polyethylene, silicone and irradiated costal cartilage [5][6][7][8].

In looksmaxxing communities the topic appears mainly in individual case threads, where members whose tip dropped or whose result looks different from what they expected ask whether a second operation, a filler or another procedure such as jaw surgery would help [9]. Research on the operation itself is largely made up of case series and single-centre reviews; it also includes psychological work on the patients who seek nasal surgery [10][11].

chain: Identify what the first rhinoplasty left behind (tip, bridge, asymmetry, airway)
Rebuild support with grafts or implants, usually through an open approach
A more balanced nasal profile and, where relevant, better breathing
angle.text: A revision aims to correct a nose that did not turn out as intended after a first operation, by repositioning or rebuilding the structures that shape the tip, bridge and nostrils. People who pursue it do so to bring the nose closer to the profile they originally wanted or to restore airflow, as described in the surgical literature [1][4].

paras: Revision rhinoplasty is defined by what comes before it: an earlier nasal operation, whether cosmetic, functional or after trauma. Wikipedia describes it as surgery to correct a failed rhinoplasty and lists typical problems as breathing deficits from over-aggressive surgery, asymmetry, collapse, a hanging columella, a pinched tip and a scooped nose [1]. Reviews describing the surgical approach organise revision problems by whether too much tissue was removed (over-resection) or too little (under-resection), and by problems from sutures or grafts [4].

Because primary surgery can weaken the cartilaginous framework, surgeons often need to reconstruct support. One review in a facial plastic surgery series advocates an open approach for most revisions because it gives better visualisation and more predictable grafting, particularly when a different surgeon performed the primary operation [4]. Another panel review covers the more severe end of the range, the severely damaged nose, in which the soft tissue envelope, the support structure and the internal lining must all be considered [12].

Common cosmetic reasons include asymmetry, a tip that is too narrow, too rotated or has lost projection, and a dorsum that is irregular or over- or under-reduced. A review of pinched nasal tip describes it as a frequent sequel of earlier surgery, in which tip-narrowing manoeuvres weaken the lateral crura and the alar margin; its authors describe lateral crural strut grafts, with or without repositioning, as a corrective technique [13]. Dorsal deficiency, often addressed with grafts in both primary and revision cases, is covered in a clinics review that favours autologous grafts for their biocompatibility and natural, lasting results, and stresses assessing overall nasofacial balance before planning [14].

The pollybeak deformity, a fullness above the tip, is cited as the indication for roughly half of all revision rhinoplasties in a review of risks and complications and in Wikipedia's rhinoplasty article [3][1].

Revisions are also performed for breathing. The same risks-and-complications review reports breathing disturbance in about 70 percent of revision patients who had earlier reduction rhinoplasty [3]. In a 72-patient series from the Laryngoscope, weakness or collapse of the upper lateral cartilages after rhinoplasty was treated with a conchal cartilage graft shaped like a butterfly; 70 patients (97 percent) reported complete resolution of airway symptoms and appearance improved in 62 (86 percent) after at least two years [15].

The best-known single-practice analysis, published in Aesthetic Surgery Journal in 2013, reviewed 369 consecutive cosmetic rhinoplasties performed in a plastic surgery group practice between 1998 and 2008; 72.7 percent used an open approach. Overall complication, dissatisfaction and revision rates were 7.9, 15.4 and 9.8 percent, and surgeons judged 87 percent of patients to have had successful anatomical correction. A previous nasal operation or facial fracture, lack of anatomical correction and postoperative complications were each associated with revision and dissatisfaction, and not addressing the tip at the primary operation was associated with higher dissatisfaction [2].

Population-level estimates vary with how revision is defined and how long patients are followed. Wikipedia gives a 5 to 20 percent range [1], and a 2007 review by Rettinger gives 5 to 15 percent and adds that the risk of complications declines with surgeon experience and that careful patient selection and attention to psychological factors can reduce dissatisfaction [3]. Wikipedia notes that smoking impairs healing and that swelling can take at least a year to resolve fully, which affects when a result can be judged [1].

Autologous septal cartilage is usually the first choice for grafting, and where septal cartilage has been used up or removed, rib or ear cartilage is the usual alternative; bone grafts and synthetic implants are further options, with Wikipedia describing implants as a choice when autologous material is not available [1]. A 2022 review of dorsal augmentation states that autologous grafts are preferred by its authors, while noting that allogeneic and synthetic sources have also been used worldwide [14].

Several long-running series describe the other materials. Godin and colleagues reviewed 309 patients (162 primary, 147 revision) who received Gore-Tex (expanded polytetrafluoroethylene) implants: 10 implants (3.2 percent) were infected and removed, a rate of 5.4 percent in revision cases against 1.2 percent in primary cases [5]. A study of porous high-density polyethylene followed 187 patients, 121 of them revisions, and reported complications in 5 (2.6 percent), all infections requiring implant removal, all in people whose skin or soft tissue was compromised by smoking, cocaine or earlier surgery [6]. A pathology study of 221 silicone implants removed in revision cases, implanted for periods from a month to 25 years, reported calcification that appeared grossly after about 5 years and 8 months and was found in about half of implants in place more than 9 years [7].

Irradiated homologous (donor) costal cartilage has also been tracked: a 2009 review of 357 patients and 1,025 grafts, with follow-up up to 24 years, reported a total complication rate of 3.25 percent and resorption of about 1 percent [8]. A 2019 clinical study of 40 patients with insufficient septal cartilage used a bone-cartilaginous unit as a graft in revision; 85 percent reported no or mild obstruction and 62.5 percent were completely or very satisfied with their nose's appearance, and the authors concluded it could replace rib grafts without added morbidity [16]. A 2008 clinical study describes perichondrium grafts in revision rhinoplasty [17].

A 2007 Laryngoscope study of revision patients at an academic centre sent questionnaires to 90 patients, of whom 46 responded about 2.5 years after surgery. Eighty-eight percent reported significant improvement in nasal performance and 79 percent said they would undergo the revision again. Satisfaction did not depend on open versus closed technique or on graft material, and was inversely related to the number of previous rhinoplasties [11].

A 2011 study in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery gave questionnaires to 226 patients seeking rhinoplasty. Thirty-three percent had at least moderate symptoms of body dysmorphic disorder. Revision rhinoplasty, aesthetic goals and psychiatric history were associated with more severe symptoms, and symptom scores correlated with the patient's own rating of the nose but not with objectively rated deformity [10]. Surgeons who describe the findings often refer to patient selection and psychological screening as part of reducing dissatisfaction [3][10].

Nose reconstruction has a long history: Wikipedia traces nasal repair through Egyptian papyri, the Sushruta tradition and Tagliacozzi's 1597 flap method, and records that John Orlando Roe performed the first modern endonasal rhinoplasty in 1887 [1]. The German surgeon Jacques Joseph (1865 to 1934), known as 'Nasenjoseph', is regarded as a pioneer of modern aesthetic rhinoplasty and argued that cosmetic surgery was worth its risks because of its effect on a person's wellbeing; his textbook Nasenplastik appeared in 1928 to 1931 [18]. Open (external) rhinoplasty was introduced by Rethi in 1934 and promoted by Padovan and later Goodman from the 1970s [1].

The implant series that still form much of the revision literature date from the 1990s and 2000s: Gore-Tex in the 1990s, porous polyethylene in 1998, silicone retrievals in 2007 and long-term irradiated cartilage data in 2009 [5][6][7][8]. In the 2020s, interest has grown in nonsurgical rhinoplasty with fillers, which a 2023 review describes as a reasonable option for well-selected patients in both primary and revision cases [19]. Wikipedia reports that videos with the hashtag #nosejobcheck passed a billion views on TikTok in 2021 [1].

In looksmaxxing forums, the nose is treated as a central facial feature, so complications after rhinoplasty are discussed within the wider debate about procedures. One looksmax.org poster described a tip that dropped back a few months after surgery for a large drooping nose and asked whether fillers or a tip rhinoplasty were needed. Replies suggested consulting the original or another surgeon about a minor closed procedure, and one member speculated that a recessed maxilla failed to support the tip and planned jaw surgery [9]. These are individual opinions, not clinical findings.

Beyond the general risks of surgery, the revision literature reports infection and removal of implants, extrusion, graft resorption, persistent obstruction and further dissatisfaction [3][5][6][7]. A 2022 case report and literature review describes a patient who needed multiple cosmetic revisions after recurrent complications, noting that septal graft difficulties are common and that surgeons should be aware of the potential future need for corrective surgery [20]. Smoking and cocaine use are linked to poorer tissue and to infection in the series above [1][6].

Human data are mostly retrospective: a revision-rate analysis of 369 cases [2], implant series with Gore-Tex [5], polyethylene [6], silicone [7] and costal cartilage [8], the butterfly graft series for valve dysfunction [15], a satisfaction survey after revision [11], a body dysmorphic disorder prevalence study [10] and a bone-cartilaginous unit study of 40 patients [16]. No randomised trial of revision rhinoplasty versus no revision has been reported in these sources.

timeline.event: Gaspare Tagliacozzi publishes a method for rebuilding the nose with an arm flap [1].
John Orlando Roe performs the first modern endonasal rhinoplasty [1].
Jacques Joseph's Nasenplastik begins publication; the full edition appears in 1931 [18].
Rethi introduces the open approach to rhinoplasty [1].
Six-year experience with Gore-Tex in rhinoplasty published [21].
Ten-year Gore-Tex series of 309 patients published [5].
Long-term satisfaction after revision rhinoplasty and the 221-case silicone implant analysis published [11][7].
Study of 226 rhinoplasty candidates reports body dysmorphic disorder symptoms in about a third [10].
Cosmetic rhinoplasty revision rates revisited (369 cases) [2].
Videos tagged #nosejobcheck pass a billion views on TikTok [1].

lore.intro: Revision appears on looksmax.org in individual case threads, where members consider the cause of an undesired result and whether to seek a second operation or a jaw procedure [9].

claims.claim: A nose tip that relapses after surgery can be caused by insufficient support from a recessed maxilla.
claims.believers: One member suggests the tip dropped back because the maxilla was too recessed to support it and says he is considering jaw surgery [9].
claims.experts: Tip problems after rhinoplasty and techniques to correct them are described in the surgical literature, for example graft reconstruction of weakened support [13][4]; no published study examines maxillary support and tip relapse.

claims.claim: A dropped tip may need only a minor closed procedure rather than a full revision.
claims.believers: A reply says that, from what they have read online, a minor closed operation would likely suffice and recommends asking the original or another surgeon [9].
claims.experts: A review of revision technique advocates an open approach for most revisions, and the choice depends on individual examination [4]. A 2007 satisfaction study found outcomes did not differ between open and closed techniques [11].

claims.claim: Fillers can correct a post-surgical nose without another operation.
claims.believers: Forum posters ask whether fillers would fix a dropped or irregular tip [9].
claims.experts: A 2023 review describes nonsurgical rhinoplasty with injectable fillers as a reasonable option for well-selected patients in primary and revision cases [19].

claims.claim: Synthetic implants give predictable results in revision.
claims.believers: Implants avoid taking cartilage from a donor site, and a number of surgeons have published long series using them [5][6].
claims.experts: Series report infection in 2.6 to 5.4 percent of revision cases depending on the material [5][6], and silicone implants showed calcification after years [7]; a dorsal augmentation review prefers autologous grafts [14].

claims.claim: Each further revision gives a worse outcome.
claims.believers: Posters considering a second or third operation discuss the cumulative toll of repeated surgery on the nose, though the looksmax.org thread cited here concerns a single case [9].
claims.experts: In a 2007 survey of revision patients, satisfaction was inversely correlated with the number of previous rhinoplasties [11].

claims.claim: Dissatisfaction with a nose reflects how objectively deformed it is.
claims.believers: People seeking surgery commonly describe a specific visible feature of the nose as the source of their distress.
claims.experts: In a study of 226 rhinoplasty candidates, symptom scores of body dysmorphic disorder correlated with the patient's own rating of the nose but not with objectively rated deformity [10].
